````text
1	<!--
2	SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Volkert de Buisonjé <volkertb@users.noreply.github.com>
3	SPDX-FileContributor: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
4	SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
5	-->
6	
7	# Generic dev container
8	
9	Debian-based dev container for agentic coding: non-root user, a broad CLI toolchain,
10	Claude Code + Codex CLI + SpecStory, and Codex wired to a llama-server on the host.
11	
12	## Prerequisite
13	
14	A `llama-server` — or any server speaking the OpenAI *Responses* API — listening on
15	**port 9931 on your host**. Choosing, tuning and starting that model server is out of scope
16	here; this container only consumes it. See *llama-server on the host* below for the one
17	host-side detail that matters (which address it binds to).
18	
19	## First run
20	
21	```bash
22	cp .devcontainer/.env.example .devcontainer/.env   # required: runArgs passes --env-file
23	devcontainer up --workspace-folder .
24	devcontainer exec --workspace-folder . bash
25	```
26	
27	VS Code, JetBrains and Zed pick the config up automatically when you open the folder.
28	
29	## What's inside
30	
31	| | |
32	|---|---|
33	| Base | `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:trixie` (Debian 13), amd64 + arm64 |
34	| User | `vscode`, uid 1000, **no route to root**, uid realigned to your host user on Linux |
35	| Tools | gcc/g++/make/cmake, gdb, Python 3 + pipx + uv, Node LTS, git, jq, ripgrep, fd, bat, fzf, xxd, sqlite3, socat, tmux, shellcheck, archives, net utils |
36	| Agents | Claude Code, Codex CLI (`codex`) |
37	| Capture | SpecStory CLI (`specstory`) |
38	
39	Everything is installed at build time — there is no `postCreateCommand`, so creating a
40	container from a built image is instant and needs no network.
41	
42	## Codex and llama-server
43	
44	`.devcontainer/codex-config.toml` is copied to `~/.codex/config.toml` during the build.
45	The one change from a host-side Codex setup: the endpoint is **`host.docker.internal`**,
46	not `127.0.0.1`, which inside a container means the container itself.
47	
48	```toml
49	model_provider = "llamacpp"
50	model = "local"               # must match llama-server's -a alias
51	model_context_window = 32768  # keep in sync with llama-server's -c
52	
53	[model_providers.llamacpp]
54	name = "llama.cpp"
55	base_url = "http://host.docker.internal:9931/v1"
56	wire_api = "responses"
57	```
58	
59	Top-level keys must stay above the `[model_providers.*]` header or TOML folds them into
60	that table. No API key is needed — a keyless local endpoint is a first-class case for
61	Codex. If your server requires one, add `env_key = "MY_VAR"` and set `MY_VAR` in `.env`.
62	
63	Verify the endpoint from inside the container before blaming Codex:
64	
65	```bash
66	curl $LLAMA_SERVER_URL/v1/responses \
67	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
68	  -d '{"model":"local","input":"say hi","stream":false}'
69	```
70	
71	A Responses-shaped object back means the integration surface is good; then just run `codex`.
72	For a one-off test against a different endpoint without editing the config,
73	`CODEX_OSS_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9931/v1` overrides Codex's built-in OSS provider.
74	
75	If Codex complains about its own sandbox, note it is already inside a container — setting
76	`sandbox_mode` in `config.toml` is the knob to reach for.
77	
78	## SpecStory
79	
80	SpecStory wraps a terminal agent and auto-saves the conversation as markdown under
81	`.specstory/history/` in the project — your bind-mounted workspace, so transcripts land on
82	your host and survive the container.
83	
84	```bash
85	specstory check          # which agents it can see
86	specstory run claude     # Claude Code, with auto-save
87	specstory run codex      # Codex, with auto-save
88	specstory watch          # save sessions from an agent you start yourself
89	specstory search <query> # search past sessions
90	```
91	
92	`specstory sync`, `specstory skills` and `specstory login` are cloud features (Pro plan);
93	everything above is local-only and needs no account.
94	
95	**Before committing `.specstory/history/`, read it.** Transcripts can contain keys, paths and
96	internal detail. Only `.specstory/debug/` is git-ignored by default.
97	
98	## llama-server on the host
99	
100	The container reaches the host as `host.docker.internal` on every OS.
101	
102	- **macOS / Windows (Docker Desktop):** works with llama-server bound to `127.0.0.1`. Nothing to do.
103	- **Linux (native Docker):** `host.docker.internal` resolves to the bridge gateway (usually
104	  `172.17.0.1`), which cannot reach a loopback-bound process. Bind llama-server to the bridge
105	  address instead — still not exposed to your LAN:
106	
107	  ```bash
108	  llama-server --host 172.17.0.1 --port 9931   # ...plus your own model/tuning flags
109	  ```
110	
111	  Binding `0.0.0.0` also works but exposes the endpoint to your network; prefer the bridge address.
112	
113	## Download verification
114	
115	Every artifact fetched during the build is authenticated, and every version is pinned —
116	pinning is what makes a checksum meaningful in the first place.
117	
118	| Artifact | How it is verified |
119	|---|---|
120	| apt packages | GPG signatures on the Debian repo metadata (apt does this itself) |
121	| uv / uvx | SHA256 from the release's `.tar.gz.sha256`, checked before install |
122	| SpecStory CLI | SHA256 from the release's `checksums.txt`, checked before install |
123	| Codex CLI | SHA256 pinned in the Dockerfile — upstream publishes none (see below) |
124	| Base image | Tag only — pin a digest to harden (see below) |
125	
126	A mismatch fails the build: each `RUN` uses `set -eux` with `sha256sum -c`, so a tampered or
127	truncated download stops the build rather than being installed.
128	
129	Codex is the exception that needs care. The `openai/codex` release publishes no `.sha256`
130	files, so `CODEX_SHA256_AMD64` / `CODEX_SHA256_ARM64` are pinned in the Dockerfile alongside
131	`CODEX_VERSION` — deliberately *not* exposed as `devcontainer.json` build args, so nobody can
132	bump the version while leaving stale digests behind. To upgrade, change all three together:
133	
134	```bash
135	V=0.156.0
136	for T in x86_64 aarch64; do
137	  curl -fsSL "https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/download/rust-v$V/codex-$T-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" \
138	    | sha256sum | sed "s|-|$T|"
139	done
140	```
141	
142	To also pin the base image, resolve its multi-arch digest — the index digest covers every
143	architecture, so this stays arch-neutral:
144	
145	```bash
146	docker buildx imagetools inspect mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:trixie | head -2
147	# then: "BASE_IMAGE": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:trixie@sha256:<digest>"
148	```
149	
150	Pinning the digest freezes OS security updates until you bump it — worth it for reproducible
151	builds, but only if you refresh it deliberately.
152	
153	## Working as root
154	
155	The container user cannot become root. There is no `sudo` or `doas`, root's password is
156	locked, every setuid/setgid bit is stripped, and `no-new-privileges` is enforced by the
157	kernel. Nothing in the container runs as root either, so there is no root process to attack.
158	
159	When you need root, open a second session **from your host**, where you already have that
160	authority. Find the container and step in:
161	
162	```bash
163	docker ps                                    # find it by image or name
164	docker exec -it -u root <container> bash
165	```
166	
167	Or, from the project folder, in one line:
168	
169	```bash
170	docker exec -it -u root "$(docker ps -q -f label=devcontainer.local_folder=$PWD)" bash
171	```
172	
173	Then work normally — you are root:
174	
175	```bash
176	apt-get update && apt-get install -y <package>
177	```
178	
179	This works because the Docker daemon *starts* that shell as root. It is not an escalation
180	from inside the container, so `no-new-privileges` does not block it, and the agent running
181	in the container has no way to do the same thing.
182	
183	**Changes made this way vanish on rebuild.** They are perfect for trying something out; once
184	you know what you need, move it into the Dockerfile so it survives and stays reproducible.
185	
186	### Re-enabling sudo (not recommended)
187	
188	Sudo is off by default. Turning it on takes **two** changes, and both are required:
189	
190	1. `"ALLOW_SUDO": "true"` in `build.args` in `devcontainer.json`
191	2. Delete the `"--security-opt=no-new-privileges:true"` line from `runArgs`
192	
193	Then rebuild. With only the first, sudo is installed but the kernel refuses to let it
194	elevate — it will fail with a permissions error, which looks like a bug and is not one.
195	
196	Stripping setuid also disables `su`, `mount`, `fusermount3`, `pkexec` and `passwd` for
197	everyone in the container. That is the intent; none are needed for normal development.
198	
199	## Security notes
200	
201	- Secrets live in `.devcontainer/.env`, which is git-ignored. `.env.example` is the tracked template.
202	- Codex talks only to your own machine; no model traffic leaves the host unless you add a hosted provider.
203	- The Docker socket is deliberately **not** mounted; an agent in the container cannot control the host engine.
204	- No path to root from inside the container, so an agent that goes wrong is confined to the
205	  `vscode` user and the bind-mounted workspace. The remaining boundary is the container itself —
206	  harden that further with Docker rootless mode or userns-remap on the host.
207	- The hardening is enforced at two levels deliberately: the image removes the tools, and
208	  `no-new-privileges` blocks the whole class of escalation even if a feature or a later
209	  `apt-get install` puts a setuid binary back.
210	
211	## Build performance
212	
213	- BuildKit cache mounts hold apt's `.deb` downloads and package lists between builds.
214	- Layers are ordered coldest first: apt, then uv, then the pinned SpecStory and Codex downloads.
215	- `codex-config.toml` is copied last, so editing it rebuilds one trivial layer, not the toolchain.
216	
217	## Other architectures
218	
219	MCR publishes amd64 and arm64 only. For riscv64, set the `BASE_IMAGE` build arg to `debian:trixie`;
220	the Dockerfile creates the `vscode` user when the base image lacks it. uv ships a `riscv64gc` build
221	and is installed there too. SpecStory and Codex publish no riscv64 binaries — those steps skip
222	themselves rather than failing the build, so you get a working container without those two tools.
223	
224	## License
225	
226	Apache-2.0 — see [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md).
227
````

Findings: I ran the connectivity tests from inside the devcontainer itself (it's up and matches this repo's `Dockerfile`/`devcontainer.json` exactly). The setup is *not* misconfigured — `host.docker.internal` correctly resolves to `172.17.0.1` (the docker0 gateway), matching the `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` in `devcontainer.json` and the README's documented Linux workaround.

ping 172.17.0.1        → works (0.03ms, ICMP fine)
nc -vz 172.17.0.1 9931 → times out
nc -vz 172.17.0.1 22   → times out (!)
```

ICMP reaches the host fine, but **every TCP port times out**, not just 9931 — even port 22, which is almost certainly listening on your host. A closed port gives "connection refused" instantly; a timeout on every port means SYN packets are being silently dropped. That's the signature of a **host-side firewall** (ufw/firewalld/nftables) blocking inbound traffic from the `docker0` bridge subnet (`172.17.0.0/16`), not a llama-server binding problem.

So: `--host 172.17.0.1 --port 9931` is correct per this repo's own docs — the fix is on the host firewall, not the bind address.

   curl http://172.17.0.1:9931/v1/models

2. **Check the firewall.** Since you're on CachyOS (Arch-based), it's likely `ufw` or `firewalld`:
   ```bash
   sudo ufw status verbose        # if ufw
   sudo firewall-cmd --state --list-all   # if firewalld
   sudo nft list ruleset          # raw nftables
   ```

3. **Allow the docker bridge subnet through**, e.g. for ufw:
   ```bash
   sudo ufw allow from 172.17.0.0/16 to any port 9931 proto tcp
   ```
   for firewalld, trust the docker0 interface or add a rich rule for the subnet/port. For raw nftables, add an ACCEPT rule for `iifname "docker0"` (or the 172.17.0.0/16 source) in the input chain before any default-drop rule.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-20 15:20:43Z)**_

Short answer: no — this has to be a host-side change, Docker can't do it for you from inside the devcontainer, and that's actually correct behavior, not a gap.

**Why Docker can't handle it:** Docker automatically manages iptables rules for traffic *it* originates — published container ports (`-p`) and container-to-internet NAT. But here the traffic flows the other way: a container reaching *out* to a process the host itself is listening on (`172.17.0.1:9931`). From the kernel's point of view that's ordinary **INPUT** traffic to the host, indistinguishable from any other host-bound connection. ufw's default-deny INPUT policy catches it, and Docker has no hook into ufw/INPUT — it only touches FORWARD/NAT for its own published ports. So there's no `devcontainer.json`/`runArgs`/Dockerfile setting that can punch this hole; a container also shouldn't be able to reach out and modify the host firewall itself (that'd be a much worse security posture than a one-time host command).

**Minimal fix, scoped to just this:**
```bash
sudo ufw allow in on docker0 to any port 9931 proto tcp
```
This only opens the port to traffic arriving *on the docker0 interface* — i.e., only your own containers can reach it, nothing from your LAN or WAN. Narrower than allowing the whole `172.17.0.0/16` subnet across all interfaces, and you don't need to share any more of your ruleset for it — it's additive and independent of whatever else is in there.

This is the same category of host-side prerequisite the README already documents for the `--host 172.17.0.1` bind address. Want me to add this ufw command as a note under the existing "llama-server on the host" section in README.md, so it's not a surprise for future you (or anyone else using this devcontainer on Linux)?

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-20 15:21:53Z)**_

Yes — pin the destination to the specific bridge IP llama-server actually binds to, instead of matching any destination address on that interface:

```bash
sudo ufw allow in on docker0 to 172.17.0.1 port 9931 proto tcp
```

This narrows the rule two ways at once: traffic must arrive on the `docker0` interface (so only containers, not your LAN/WAN) **and** be destined for `172.17.0.1:9931` specifically — not any other address the host might also answer on. If the host has other addresses reachable from `docker0` (extra bridge networks, VPN interfaces, etc.), those stay unaffected by this rule.

_**User (2026-09-20 15:26:42Z)**_

Is the Docker bridge gateway always `172.17.0.1`? Or at least in the vast majority of cases? If not, is it worth emphasizing to double-check what `

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-20 15:27:06Z)**_

Good catch — no, `172.17.0.1` isn't guaranteed. It's Docker's default `docker0` bridge address, and it holds in most single-host setups (including this project's, since `devcontainer.json` has no custom network config, so it lands on the default bridge). But it can differ if:

- that subnet was already taken when Docker was first installed (Docker walks its default address-pool list until it finds a free one — `172.18.0.0/16`, `172.19.0.0/16`, etc.)
- `/etc/docker/daemon.json` sets custom `default-address-pools`
- a project *does* define its own network (e.g. via docker-compose) — different projects then get different gateways

The good news: `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway` in `devcontainer.json` already resolves this correctly and dynamically, whatever the actual gateway is — no hardcoding there. The only place the literal `172.17.0.1` is hardcoded is the README's example commands, which readers copy-paste verbatim. That's worth flagging so people don't hit exactly the confusing timeout you just debugged, for a different reason (wrong IP instead of firewall).

Let me update the README to tell readers to verify it first.

_**User (2026-09-20 15:36:03Z)**_

Any conventions or best practices w.r.t. ufw description/comment text, i.e. whether they should be capitalized or not?

---

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-20 15:36:19Z)**_

There's no enforced convention from `ufw`/iptables itself — the comment is a free-form string (iptables' comment match module caps it at 256 bytes; ufw doesn't lowercase or reformat it). So capitalization is purely a style choice, not a technical requirement.

In practice, sysadmin docs split roughly two ways:
- **Short, lowercase, telegraphic** (e.g. Ubuntu wiki / DigitalOcean tutorial style): `comment 'allow ssh'`, `comment 'allow http from lan'`
- **Capitalized, sentence-like** (common in AWS security-group descriptions, some enterprise runbooks): `comment 'Allow SSH from office VPN'`

Neither is "more correct." The one practical guideline worth following: **be consistent across your own ruleset**, since `ufw status verbose` prints every rule's comment in a column and mixed casing looks sloppy there.

The current text — `Allow access to local llama-server from Docker containers` — is capitalized, imperative, no trailing period, which matches the AWS-SG-description convention and reads cleanly in `ufw status verbose`. I'd leave it as-is unless you already have other `ufw` rules on this host with a different casing style you want to match — in which case, match those instead.

 - **macOS / Windows (Docker Desktop):** works with llama-server bound to `127.0.0.1`. Nothing to do.

+- **Linux (native Docker):** `host.docker.internal` resolves to the bridge gateway, which
+  cannot reach a loopback-bound process. That gateway is `172.17.0.1` in the common case
+  (Docker's default `docker0` bridge, which is what this project's containers use, since
+  nothing here defines a custom network) — but it isn't guaranteed: Docker picks a different
+  subnet if `172.17.0.0/16` was already taken when Docker was first installed, or if
+  `/etc/docker/daemon.json` sets custom `default-address-pools`. Verify it from inside the
+  container before copying the commands below verbatim:
 
   ```bash
+  # Run this inside the container:
+  getent hosts host.docker.internal
+  ```
+
+  If that prints something other than `172.17.0.1`, substitute your actual address in the
+  commands that follow. Bind llama-server to that bridge address — still not exposed to your LAN:
+
+  ```bash
+  # Run this in the host environment:
   llama-server --host 172.17.0.1 --port 9931   # ...plus your own model/tuning flags
   ```
 
+  A host firewall (e.g. `ufw`) can still block this: binding to `172.17.0.1` is an
+  ordinary listening address as far as the kernel's INPUT chain is concerned, and
+  Docker does not manage that chain — it only handles traffic it originates itself
+  (published container ports, NAT), not a container reaching a host-bound process.
+  If `curl` from inside the container times out (not "connection refused") even
+  though the port is listening, allow it explicitly, scoped to just the docker
+  bridge interface and this address:
+
+  ```bash
+  # Run this in the host environment:
+  sudo ufw allow in on docker0 to 172.17.0.1 port 9931 proto tcp comment 'Allow access to local llama-server from Docker containers'
+  ```
+
+  This persists across reboots like any other `ufw` rule. To remove it later:
+
+  ```bash
+  # Run this in the host environment:
+  sudo ufw delete allow in on docker0 to 172.17.0.1 port 9931 proto tcp comment 'Allow access to local llama-server from Docker containers'
+  ```
+
   Binding `0.0.0.0` also works but exposes the endpoint to your network; prefer the bridge address.
